newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan dollar drops again, lowest close since '88.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan dollar drops again, lowest close since '88.

text.p: The Taiwan dollar plunged anew against the U.S. dollar on Thursday, notching its lowest close since 1988 on the greenback's persistent strength overseas and the central bank's non-interference, dealers said.
The local unit, which facing intense selling pressure for the third straight session, closed at its intraday low of T$28.70 against Wednesday's T$28.480 finish.
Turnover through dealers was heavy at US$428 million.
Against a backdrop of analyst comments that the rate could test T$29, dealers said the market appeared to be testing the central bank's bottom line -- and finding little resistance.
"The central bank, as in the past two days, did not intervene today," said one dealer.
"The market wants to test how far the central bank will allow the Taiwan dollar to depreciate," the dealer said.

The central bank on Tuesday allowed the Taiwan dollar to fall below T$28 for the first time since 1989, sparking a flood of local dollar selling spurred on by the greenback's strength against the yen and other major currencies.
The currency's latest drop came even as the central bank was behind closed doors holding a quarterly meeting.
Market experts said the depreciation was surely a key agendy item, but predicted before the meeting that the central bank was unlikely to adjust its monetary policy in the near term.
The central bank on Wednesday reiterated its pledge to keep its hands off of Taiwan's foreign exchange market, saying it would respect market forces.

"U.S. dollar buying remained very strong throughout the session. Investors who had thought the Taiwan dollar slide would not last are starting to worry that the depreciation trend will continue," one dealer said.
Another dealer said the market would be closely watching the outcome of the bank meeting, which started at 0700 GMT.
"If the central bank still says it will respect market forces, the Taiwan dollar may fall to T$29 tomorrow," she said.
The central bank planned a news briefing after the meeting.

Dealers maintain that despite its tumble, the Taiwan dollar clearly was not suffering from -- or vulnerable to -- the kind of speculative attacks that have shocked several southeast Asian currencies in July, particularly the Thai baht.

While those countries' currencies fell precipitously despite strident public opposition by their central banks, Taiwan's central bank has been seen by experts as tacitly welcoming, even encouraging, a well-tempered depreciation in the interest of stronger exports -- Taiwan's economic life-blood.
They say Taiwan's central bank, boasting imposing foreign exchange reserves of over US$90 billion, could easily defend the currency as it often has at times of political uncertainty.

The bank's clout was never clearer than during a long spate in 1995-96 when it held the Taiwan dollar above T$27.5 despite military intimidation by rival China that triggered a run on foreign exchange and gold and a flood of capital outflows.
Within two months after that crisis ease, the central bank said it was no longer defending T$27.5, setting the currency onto a long, languid depreciation that has yet to play out.
-- Alice Hung, Taipei Newsroom (2-5080815)
